label: The Pseudosphere and the Hyperbolic Plane
notes: Open by framing the chapter question that runs through printed pages 51 to 64: how do we make a plane of constant negative curvature measurable? Beltrami's pseudosphere is the answer, a real surface obeying hyperbolic rules that we can sketch and quantify.

label: The Tractrix
notes: Introduce the tractrix through the dragged-weight story. Emphasize the one property that defines it: the tangent segment from the curve to the axis keeps a constant length. Stress that this geometric constraint, not the formula, is what we will spin into a surface.

label: Building the Pseudosphere
notes: Rotate the tractrix about its asymptote to sweep the pseudosphere. Contrast it explicitly with the sphere: where the sphere bulges outward everywhere, the pseudosphere saddles. Point out the meridians and parallels that give the surface a natural coordinate grid for later metric work.

label: Constant Negative Curvature
notes: Show that opposite bending of the two principal directions forces the curvature product negative. Compute it to the constant minus one over the squared radius, and normalize the radius so the surface carries curvature exactly minus one, the intrinsic invariant the lecture keeps tracking.

label: Conformal Coordinates
notes: Explain that a conformal chart rescales the surface by one common factor at each point, preserving angles. Derive that the factor is one over the height squared, which unrolls the pseudosphere onto a strip of the upper half plane and hands us the model metric.

label: The Beltrami-Poincare Half-Plane
notes: Define the half plane with its metric dividing Euclidean length by height. Drive home that the real axis sits infinitely far away because tiny steps near it cost unbounded hyperbolic length. This single rule contains all of hyperbolic trigonometry in compact form.

label: Hyperbolic Distance and Discs
notes: Use the vertical-distance formula to show distance counts ratios of heights, not differences. Two discs of equal hyperbolic radius therefore look completely different to the Euclidean eye. The lesson is to trust the intrinsic measurement, not the visual size, in any model.

label: Geodesics as Semicircles
notes: Identify hyperbolic straight lines as vertical rays and semicircles centred on the axis, each meeting the boundary orthogonally. Offer the optical interpretation: light in a medium whose speed grows with height bends along these arcs, so Snell's law reproduces hyperbolic geodesics exactly.

label: The Angle of Parallelism
notes: Drop a perpendicular of length d to a line and find the limiting parallel ray. Give Lobachevsky's formula and stress the angle is always less than ninety degrees, shrinking as d grows. This quantifies precisely how parallels fail in hyperbolic geometry.

label: The Beltrami-Poincare Disc
notes: Map the half plane to the unit disc by a Mobius transformation and write the disc metric. Show geodesics become diameters and arcs orthogonal to the boundary circle. Highlight how the entire infinite hyperbolic plane is compressed into a finite, highly symmetric picture.

label: Comparing the Two Models
notes: Stress that the half plane and the disc are one geometry in two costumes, linked by an angle-preserving Mobius map. Recommend the half plane for boundary and horocycle work and the disc for rotational symmetry and tilings, since each exposes different features.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: Recap the chain from tractrix to pseudosphere to conformal chart to the two Poincare models, all carrying curvature minus one. Close by previewing the next move: allowing curvature to vary from point to point, which opens the general theory of Riemannian metrics.
